issues.legal_issue: A contempt proceeding is initiated when the court, after applying its mind and forming a prima facie view that contempt proceedings are warranted, calls on the alleged contemnor to show cause why they should not be punished; a notice asking only why proceedings should be initiated is not enough.
material_facts: The appellant alleged that the respondents’ employees demolished construction despite an undertaking to preserve it while the appellant’s writ petition was pending.
The court’s first notice asked the respondents to show cause why contempt proceedings should not be initiated; that notice preceded initiation of proceedings.

A later signed order directed the respondents to show cause why they should not be punished for disobeying the court’s order. The court treated that order as showing that it had applied its mind and formed the view that a case for contempt proceedings was made out.
The later notice was issued within one year of the alleged demolition. An earlier order that had been dictated but not signed was disregarded.
issues.conclusion: The proceedings were initiated by the later notice calling on the respondents to show cause why they should not be punished, and that initiation occurred within the applicable period. The bar did not apply; the appeal was allowed and the proceedings restored for hearing, without deciding whether contempt had in fact occurred.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 bars a court from initiating contempt proceedings after one year from the alleged contempt. Initiation requires a conscious application of the court’s mind and a decision that a prima facie case for contempt proceedings exists. Filing an application, receiving a reference, issuing a routine notice, or asking why proceedings should be initiated is anterior to initiation; calling on the alleged contemnor to show cause why they should not be punished amounts to initiation. Section 20 limits jurisdiction, rather than operating as ordinary limitation, so Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply. The Court relied on Baradakanta Mishra v. Mr. Justice Gatikrushna Misra, Chief Justice of the Orissa High Court, and referred to The Advocate General v. A.V. Koteswara Rao, Kishan Singh v. T. Anjaiah, and Dineshbhai A. Parikh v. Kripalu Co-operative Housing Society.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and court_applied_mind_to_material and court_found_prima_facie_case and notice_calls_for_punishment and notice_issued_within_one_year

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter before the court is a proceeding seeking action for alleged contempt.
predicates.court_applied_mind_to_material: The court considered the allegations and material before it before deciding what action to take.
predicates.court_found_prima_facie_case: The court formed the view that the material disclosed a prima facie case for contempt proceedings.
predicates.notice_calls_for_punishment: The court called on the alleged contemnor to show cause why they should not be punished, rather than only why proceedings should be initiated.
predicates.notice_issued_within_one_year: The court issued the notice calling for a response to the proposed punishment within one year of the alleged contempt.

issues.definition: In a contempt proceeding, a punishment-show-cause notice issued within one year after the court considers the material and finds a prima facie case means the proceedings are not time-barred.
